st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source does not assess AI performance directly, but materially extends the cluster’s work-redesign argument by identifying the broad human capabilities that redesigned workflows and professional-development systems should preserve. Its nationwide survey distinguishes immediate foundations from skills acquired over time, supporting selective task allocation rather than treating legal work as a uniform bundle that technology can replace.
qs: If a foundation is classified as either “necessary in the      short term” or “must be acquired over time,” it is ultimately necessary at some point in time; the difference in these      two options represents the degree of urgency for the new lawyer in gaining proficiency in the foundation.

kp.k: National survey identifies foundations for entry-level legal practice
kp.d: Gerkman and Cornett report a survey administered through partnerships in 37 states during the fourth quarter of 2014 and first quarter of 2015. It was sent to an estimated 780,694 lawyers and received 24,137 valid responses from attorneys with offices in all 50 states. Respondents rated 147 foundations, distinguishing immediate necessity, necessity over time, advantage without necessity, and irrelevance. This is evidence about practitioners’ expectations for lawyer formation, not a study of AI or observed effects of AI adoption.
qs: We asked respondents to rate the necessity of 147 foundations (plus two questions that allowed write-in responses)
During survey design, we opted to divide the 147 foundations into 15 categories to create a more respondent-friendly survey experience.

kp.k: Employment and perceived preparedness gaps motivate reform
kp.d: The report cites ABA outcomes for 2015 graduates ten months after graduation: almost 40% lacked full-time jobs requiring a law license, only 70% obtained full-time jobs requiring a license or preferring a JD, and one in four did not report any job. It separately reports BARBRI’s finding that 71% of third-year students considered themselves sufficiently skilled to practice, compared with 23% of practitioners assessing new lawyers, and Lexis Nexis’s finding that 95% of surveyed hiring partners and associates believed recent graduates lacked key practical skills. These are external employment data and perceptions, not findings that preparedness caused unemployment.
qs: Only 23% of practitioners believe new lawyers have sufficient skills to practice.
The employment gap is exacerbated by another gap: the gap between the skillset lawyers want in new graduates and the skillset lawyers believe new graduates have.

kp.k: The whole lawyer combines three kinds of foundations
kp.d: The authors distinguish characteristics, professional competencies useful across vocations, and discipline-specific legal skills. Of the survey items, 28% addressed characteristics, 45% professional competencies, and 27% legal skills. Their whole-lawyer framework rejects a choice between technical training and intellectual development and proposes a character quotient alongside intelligence and emotional intelligence; the report does not present CQ as a measured individual score.
qs: “Characteristics” are foundations capturing features or qualities (such as sociability).
“Professional competencies” are skills seen as useful across vocations (such as managing meetings effectively).
“Legal skills” are those traditionally understood to be required for the specific discipline of law (such as preparing a case on appeal).
Our findings suggest that lawyers also require some level of character quotient (CQ).

kp.k: Character is more urgent than many technical skills
kp.d: Using a threshold of at least half of respondents, 76% of characteristics, 46% of professional competencies, and 40% of legal skills were classified as necessary immediately. These percentages describe shares of foundations within each type, not shares of respondents preferring character over skills. The report finds statistically significant differences in urgency (χ²(2) = 13.17, p = 0.001), while differences in eventual necessity—98% of legal skills, 95% of characteristics, and 86% of professional competencies—were not statistically significant (χ²(4) = 7.20, p = 0.125).
qs: Perhaps unsurprisingly, respondents considered an overwhelming majority (92%) of the foundations to be necessary; that is, 135 out of the 147 foundations.
Specifically, fewer than half of the legal skills we asked about—just 40%—were identified as necessary right out of law school.
This is not to suggest that legal skills were viewed as unnecessary by respondents.

kp.k: Reliability and interpersonal conduct dominate immediate expectations
kp.d: The ten foundations most frequently rated immediately necessary contained no legal skills. They included confidentiality (96.1%), punctuality (95.4%), honoring commitments (93.7%), integrity and trustworthiness (92.3%), courtesy and respect (91.9%), attentive listening (91.5%), prompt responses (91.0%), diligence (88.4%), work ethic (88.1%), and attention to detail (87.8%). These findings identify entry-level expectations rather than directly measured predictors of career success.
qs: legal skills make no appearance in the top ten foundations new lawyers need for success right out of law school.

kp.k: Core legal reasoning remains an immediate requirement
kp.d: The report does not recommend deferring all technical formation. Effective legal research was rated immediately necessary by 83.7%, identifying relevant facts and legal issues by 71.0%, gathering facts by 67.3%, legal reasoning and argument by 65.0%, and critically evaluating arguments by 55.4%. The authors note that several of these foundations already receive substantial attention in law schools.

kp.k: Specialized practice skills develop over time
kp.d: Among litigation respondents, drafting pleadings, motions, and briefs (72%), written discovery (65%), and interviewing clients and witnesses (50%) met the immediate-necessity threshold. Among transaction respondents, preparing client responses (51%) and drafting contracts and agreements (50%) did so. Other abilities were commonly assigned to later development: specialization (73.7%), risk mitigation strategies (70.0%), preparing a case for trial (65.5%), and in-court trial advocacy (64.4%). Litigation and transaction questions were restricted to respondents reporting the relevant practice.
qs: Questions in this section were presented only to lawyers who indicated they had a litigation practice.
Questions in this section were presented only to lawyers who indicated they had a transaction practice.
Almost three-quarters (74%) of respondents considered the development of expertise in a particular area as something that must be acquired over time.

kp.k: Technology learning outweighs immediate sophisticated technology deployment
kp.d: In this 2014–15 survey, 58.1% rated learning and using relevant technologies effectively as immediately necessary, and 33.5% assigned it to acquisition over time. Using technology to increase the value or sophistication of services was immediately necessary to 24.8% and to be acquired over time to 46.4%. Online law-related professional activity and networking was rated advantageous but unnecessary by 52.0%. These findings concern technology generally, not generative AI.
qs: a majority (58%) of respondents did consider the ability to learn and use relevant technologies effectively as necessary right out of law school.
Conversely, engaging in online law-related professional activity and networking was seen by a majority (52%) as advantageous, but not necessary.

kp.k: Self-management and collaborative learning underpin early practice
kp.d: Immediate expectations included responsibility for actions and results (82.2%), knowing when to engage a supervisor or seek advice (75.2%), responsiveness to feedback (71.7%), teamwork (72.9%), managing multiple tasks (72.8%), and maintaining high-quality work (72.0%). Stress and crisis management were also widely regarded as necessary immediately or over time. This supports the authors’ broader account of professional formation beyond legal technique alone.
qs: taking individual responsibility for actions and results being the foundation most commonly identified as necessary right out of law school (82%).
Notably, nearly three in four respondents (73%) indicated that the ability to work collaboratively as part of a team was necessary in the short term.

kp.k: Law schools should measure broader learning outcomes
kp.d: The authors recommend that graduates demonstrate facility with the 77 foundations classified as immediately necessary. Schools should collaborate with employers on measurable outcomes, embed relevant courses in curricula, support individual learning plans, and reconsider admissions criteria beyond intelligence. They situate these recommendations within ABA accreditation standards revised in August 2014 and applicable to the incoming 2016–17 class, requiring learning outcomes, assessment, and program evaluation.
qs: We believe legal educators and law schools should strive to ensure each and every law school graduate can demonstrate some level of facility with these foundations.
The new standards will be applied to the incoming class of 2016-17.

kp.k: Hiring incentives must reinforce educational reform
kp.d: The authors argue that hiring on law-school prestige, class rank, and law review perpetuates incentives inconsistent with employers’ stated preferences. They report that respondents regarded experience—including legal employment, clinics, and experiential education—as helpful evidence of desired foundations, while law review ranked second least useful. Detailed hiring results were reserved for a future report. Their recommendation is to align selection throughout hiring with the broader foundations employers say they want.
qs: the gap between what the profession says it wants in new lawyers and the way the profession actually hires new lawyers.
overwhelmingly they singled out experience, including legal employment, clinics, experiential education.
We will explore these results in full in a future report

kp.k: Improved employment and public trust are predicted benefits
kp.d: The authors predict that coordinated changes to education and hiring will improve graduate employment, client service, and public trust. These are conditional expectations attached to their reform proposals, not outcomes demonstrated by the survey.
qs: For legal education to make meaningful strides, law schools and legal employers must work together.

When law schools educate students toward learning outcomes developed with feedback from employers and employers hire based on what they say they want, we will see law school graduates with high character quotients who embody the whole lawyer, we will see the employment gap shrink, we will see clients who are served by the most competent lawyers the system can produce, and we will ultimately see public trust in our system expand.
